title: A hybrid learning system for recognizing user tasks from desktop activities and email messages
research_question: Can machine-learning models automatically infer a user's current task from desktop activity or an incoming email with sufficiently high precision to reduce the need for manual task selection?
methodology: The paper presents TaskPredictor as a component of TaskTracer, with separate predictors for desktop window/document sequences and incoming email messages. Email classification uses features derived from sender, recipients, and subject words, while desktop classification uses words associated with applications and accessed resources; mutual-information feature selection reduces the feature space. The authors compare Naive Bayes, support vector machines, and a hybrid in which Naive Bayes supplies a confidence estimate and an SVM chooses the class, with confidence thresholds allowing the system to abstain. Evaluation uses TaskTracer data from nine users, although desktop-sequence evaluation is limited to two faculty users and email evaluation uses manually task-sorted messages from the remaining participants.

key_findings.finding: Incoming email can be classified into a user's predefined work tasks using sender, recipient, and subject information with high precision at useful but incomplete coverage.
The email predictor reached about 92% precision at roughly 66% coverage with the hybrid classifier in the reported evaluation.
The hybrid Naive-Bayes/SVM design generally matched or exceeded the best individual classifier's precision at comparable coverage.
Using approximately 200 mutual-information-selected features was sufficient for the evaluated email and desktop predictors and avoided unnecessary feature growth.
Words from the email body did not provide additional predictive benefit in the authors' experiments beyond sender, recipient, and subject features.
Prediction errors increase when a user begins a new task for which the classifier has little training data.

limitations: The participant pool is small and largely drawn from one academic environment, limiting external validity for broader enterprises.
Desktop-sequence evaluation uses data from only two users because of privacy and data-quality constraints.
Email ground truth was created by participants manually sorting sampled messages into folders corresponding to TaskTracer tasks rather than by observing naturally evolving business-event identities.
The study classifies individual messages into predefined user tasks; it does not directly link separate email or chat threads into a common evolving business matter.
The models largely treat classification examples independently even though task switching is inherently sequential; the authors identify temporal models as future work.
Performance degrades for newly created tasks that have few training examples and may reuse resources associated with older tasks.
The private user data and email corpus are not released as a reproducible public dataset.
raw_claims: TaskTracer associates computer resources such as files, email messages, contacts, and web pages with user-defined activities.
Users can forget to change the declared task when they switch work contexts.
TaskPredictor attempts to infer the current task automatically.
The email predictor uses sender, recipient, and subject-word features.
The authors found no useful additional predictive value from email-body words in their experiments.
Mutual-information ranking is used to select a compact subset of features.
The hybrid classifier uses Naive Bayes to estimate confidence and an SVM to choose the predicted task.
A confidence threshold permits the predictor to abstain when its prediction is uncertain.
Email evaluation uses a chronological split between training and test messages.
The hybrid email predictor achieved high precision while making predictions for only part of the messages.
Newly introduced tasks are particularly difficult because little task-specific training data exists.
The paper notes that sequential or temporal modeling could improve future versions of the system.
